newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Malan says perfectly calm about Brazil trade, C/A.
newsitem.headline: Malan says perfectly calm about Brazil trade, C/A.

text.p: Brazil Finance Minister Pedro Malan, predicting a current account gap of less than 3.0 percent for 1996, said he was perfectly calm about Brazil's external accounts.

In an interview late Monday with Reuters, Malan said he saw no reason for contractionist or expansionist economic policies in 1997 and that he expected "reasonable" gross domestic product growth of 4.0-4.5 next year compared with about 3.1 percent this year.

"The deficit in the current account will be a maximum of 3.0 percent of GDP, no, it will be less than 3.0 percent. It isn't high by any relevant international comparison and is being financed by resources of better and better quality," Malan said.
"We are not worried at all about the the balance of the external accounts, the balance of payments," he said.
"It doesn't mean there won't be any problems, it means there won't be any problems we can't deal with. A deficit in the order of 3.0 percent of GDP is easily financed by Brazil."
Malan said he expected GDP growth of 4.0-4.5 percent next year, which he considered "reasonable".

"There's no need for a policy of stop and go," he said. "We will have growth of 4.0-4.5 percent next year, which I think reasonable without the need for the government to adopt any kind of measure to stimulate expansion or contraction."
The minister said he was convinced that measures adopted to spur exports -- such as exemption from so-called ICMS tax and the revival of export insurance -- would take effect next year.
He also noted that imports were mainly composed of capital goods and primary and intermediary goods, which he said "represents a future increase in productivity and thus greater export potential".
Noting recent wholesale price inflation figures, Malan said it looked like Brazil might post single-digit wholesale inflation in 1996, the first time since 1957.
